"Impose on" is a phrasal verb — a verb made of two parts: impose + the preposition on. You can also say "impose upon" (same meaning, slightly more formal). Both are correct and used interchangeably.

At the heart of this phrase is the word impose, which means to place or force something on someone without their free agreement. The "on" simply tells you who that something is being placed on.
The Two Core Meanings

Meaning 1 — To burden someone / To take unfair advantage of their kindness

This is the most common, everyday meaning, and the one you'll encounter most often.

When you "impose on" someone, you are asking more of them than is fair, or you are using their time, energy, or generosity in a way that is inconvenient or uncomfortable for them — often relying on the fact that they are too kind or polite to say no.

The key idea: The person being imposed on didn't truly have a free choice. They feel obligated, pressured, or burdened.

Examples:

  • "I hate to impose on you, but could you babysit my kids tonight?"
  • "He kept imposing on his roommate by eating his food without permission."
  • "She imposed on her neighbor's kindness by asking for a ride to work every single day."
  • "I don't want to impose on your weekend, so I'll figure it out myself."
  • "Stop imposing on your friends — they have their own problems to deal with."

Notice the extremely common phrase "I don't want to impose." People say this when they're about to ask a favor and want to politely acknowledge that the request might be a burden. It shows self-awareness.

Meaning 2 — To force something on someone without their choice

In this meaning, "impose on" means to force something onto someone — a rule, a belief, a punishment, a tax, a restriction — without giving them a say in the matter.

The key idea: Something is being applied to someone from the outside, by a person or authority who has the power (or thinks they have the right) to do so.

Examples:

  • "You shouldn't impose your personal beliefs on other people."
  • "The government imposed new taxes on its citizens."
  • "The judge imposed a heavy sentence on the criminal."
  • "Stop trying to impose your taste in music on everyone around you."
  • "The dictator imposed his will on the entire nation."
  • "New trade restrictions were imposed on the country."
  • "Don't impose your definition of success on your children."
How the Two Meanings Differ Grammatically

This is a neat trick to help you tell the two meanings apart:

  • In Meaning 1, there is usually no object between "impose" and "on":

→ "She imposed on her friend." (= She burdened her friend)

  • In Meaning 2, there is always an object (the thing being forced) between "impose" and "on":

→ "She imposed her opinion on her friend." (= She forced her opinion on her friend)

This small grammatical difference is a reliable signal to identify which meaning is being used.
The Feeling Behind the Word (Connotation)

"Impose on" almost always carries a negative feeling. It suggests:

  • Unfairness
  • A lack of respect for someone's time, freedom, or comfort
  • Someone overstepping their boundaries or abusing another person's goodwill

Whether someone is imposing on your time, your kindness, or your freedom — the word signals that something is wrong. Something is being pushed onto someone who didn't ask for it or didn't fully agree to it.
Grammar: How to Use It in Sentences

Pattern 1 (Meaning 1):
Subject + impose on + person
→ "Please don't impose on your colleagues."
→ "He is always imposing on others."

Pattern 2 (Meaning 2):
Subject + impose + [thing] + on + person
→ "Don't impose your rules on the whole group."
→ "Heavy fines were imposed on the company."

Passive voice (very common, especially in news and formal writing):
→ "Sanctions were imposed on the country."
→ "A curfew was imposed on the city."

"Impose upon" = "impose on" — same meaning, slightly more formal or literary:
→ "I don't wish to impose upon your valuable time."
The Related Noun: "Imposition"

The noun form of "impose on" is imposition. Knowing it doubles your ability to use this word family.

  • "What an imposition!" = "What an unfair burden / What an unreasonable ask!"
  • "Asking him to work every weekend was a real imposition."
  • "I hope my visit wasn't too much of an imposition."
  • "Accepting such conditions would be an imposition on our freedom."

People naturally switch between the verb and the noun, so recognizing both helps you follow conversations and written text easily.
A Critical Confusion to Avoid: "Imposing" ≠ "Imposing On"

The adjective "imposing" means something entirely different — it means large, grand, or commanding in appearance. It has nothing to do with "impose on."

  • "The palace was an imposing structure." (= It looked grand and impressive.)
  • "She cut an imposing figure in the courtroom." (= She appeared powerful and commanding.)

Do not mix these up. "Imposing" as an adjective is a compliment. "Imposing on someone" is a criticism.
Synonyms

For Meaning 1 (burdening someone):

  • Take advantage of
  • Put upon
  • Burden
  • Inconvenience
  • Exploit someone's goodwill

For Meaning 2 (forcing something on someone):

  • Force on / Force upon
  • Foist on (means to push something unwanted onto someone)
  • Inflict on
  • Thrust upon
  • Dictate to
Common Collocations (Natural Word Pairings)

These are phrases you will regularly see "impose on" used with in real life:

  • Impose on someone's time → "I don't want to impose on your time."
  • Impose on someone's kindness / generosity → "He imposed on her generosity one too many times."
  • Impose restrictions on → "New restrictions were imposed on travel."
  • Impose sanctions on → "Sanctions were imposed on the regime."
  • Impose one's will on → "He tried to impose his will on the whole team."
  • Impose one's views / beliefs / values on → "Don't impose your values on others."
  • Impose a sentence / fine / penalty on → "The court imposed a large fine on the company."
  • Impose a curfew / ban / tax on → "A ban was imposed on public gatherings."
A Brief Note on a Rare, Older Meaning

In older, more literary or formal English, "impose on" could also mean to deceive or trick someone. You might encounter this in classic novels or historical texts.

  • "He imposed on the court with forged documents." (= He deceived the court.)

This usage is rare in modern everyday English, so you don't need to use it yourself — but you may occasionally come across it in older writing.
Quick Summary

To keep it simple without a table — here's the takeaway in plain words:

"Impose on" means either (1) to unfairly burden someone or take advantage of their goodwill, or (2) to force something — a rule, belief, tax, punishment — onto someone without their free choice. In both cases, the word carries a negative feeling: something is being pushed onto someone who didn't truly welcome it. The noun form is imposition, and "impose upon" means exactly the same thing with a slightly more formal tone.
